---
title: "ROC curve and AUC"
description: "Measuring how well a model ranks positives above negatives, across all thresholds."
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from modelperf.metrics import auc_rank, auc_trapezoid, gini_from_auc, roc_points, threshold_metrics
from modelperf.models import binary_predictions
from modelperf.plots import MODEL_COLORS, INK_SECONDARY, MUTED, plot_roc, use_style

use_style()
b = binary_predictions()
y = b["y"]
auc = {m: auc_rank(y, b[m]) for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")}
```

**Question answered:** does the model rank policies with a claim above policies
without one?

## Every threshold at once

On the [previous page](confusion-matrix.qmd), each threshold gave one
confusion matrix and with it one pair of rates:

- the **true positive rate** (TPR, recall): the share of claims we flag, and
- the **false positive rate** (FPR): the share of non-claims we flag.

The **ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic) plots this pair for
every possible threshold. A very high threshold flags nothing: the curve starts
at (0, 0). Lowering it flags more and more policies until everything is flagged,
at (1, 1). The marked points are the thresholds from the previous page:

```{python}
#| label: fig-roc-gbm
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve of the GBM, with three thresholds marked."
ax = plot_roc(y, {"GBM": b["GBM"]},
              operating_points={"t = 0.2": ("GBM", 0.2), "t = 0.1": ("GBM", 0.1), "t = 0.05": ("GBM", 0.05)})
```

The diagonal is a model that ranks at random: whatever share of policies it
flags, it flags the same share of claims and non-claims. The further a curve
bulges towards the top-left corner, the better the model ranks.

## Building the curve by hand

Ten policies, sorted by predicted probability, make the construction concrete:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-toy
#| tbl-cap: "Ten toy policies and the ROC point after lowering the threshold to each score."
#| code-fold: false
toy_y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0])
toy_p = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
toy_roc = roc_points(toy_y, toy_p)
toy_roc.assign(outcome=np.r_[np.nan, toy_y])
```

Each time the threshold passes a policy, the curve takes a step: **up** by
1/4 if it had a claim (4 positives), **right** by 1/6 if it didn't
(6 negatives). A perfect model would go straight up first, then right.

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve of the ten toy policies. Shaded: the area under the curve."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 4))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, linewidth=1)
ax.fill_between(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"], color=MODEL_COLORS["GLM"], alpha=0.1, linewidth=0)
ax.plot(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"], color=MODEL_COLORS["GLM"], marker="o", markersize=6,
        markeredgecolor="#fcfcfb", markeredgewidth=2)
ax.set(xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.02), aspect="equal")
toy_auc = auc_trapezoid(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"])
ax.annotate(f"AUC = {toy_auc:.3f}", (0.55, 0.3), color=INK_SECONDARY)
```

## AUC: two interpretations

The **area under the ROC curve** (AUC) condenses the curve into one number
between 0 and 1. It has two equivalent readings.

**1. Geometric.** The area under the curve: 1.0 for a perfect model, 0.5 for
random ranking (the diagonal).

**2. Probabilistic.** The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen
policy *with* a claim gets a higher score than a randomly chosen policy
*without* one (ties count half):

$$
\text{AUC} = P\left(\hat p_i > \hat p_j \mid y_i = 1,\ y_j = 0\right).
$$

The second reading makes clear that **AUC measures ranking only**. It's the
Mann–Whitney U statistic, and it can be computed from ranks without drawing
any curve. On the toy example, `{python} str(int(round(toy_auc * 24)))` of the
4 × 6 = 24 (claim, no-claim) pairs are ordered correctly:
`{python} str(int(round(toy_auc * 24)))`/24 = `{python} f"{toy_auc:.3f}"`.

On the real test set, both computations agree, and so does a brute-force
check that samples random pairs:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-auc-check
#| tbl-cap: "AUC of the GBM, computed three ways."
#| code-fold: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
p_pos = b.loc[y == 1, "GBM"].to_numpy()
p_neg = b.loc[y == 0, "GBM"].to_numpy()
i, j = rng.integers(len(p_pos), size=1_000_000), rng.integers(len(p_neg), size=1_000_000)
sampled = np.mean(p_pos[i] > p_neg[j]) + 0.5 * np.mean(p_pos[i] == p_neg[j])

roc = roc_points(y, b["GBM"])
pd.Series({
    "Area under the curve (trapezoids)": auc_trapezoid(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"]),
    "Rank statistic (Mann–Whitney)": auc_rank(y, b["GBM"]),
    "1 million random pairs": sampled,
}, name="AUC").round(4).to_frame()
```

### Gini coefficient

Credit scoring and insurance usually report the **Gini coefficient** (also
called the accuracy ratio or Somers' D) instead:

$$
\text{Gini} = 2 \cdot \text{AUC} - 1.
$$

It rescales AUC so that random ranking scores 0 and perfect ranking scores 1.
The GBM's AUC of `{python} f"{auc['GBM']:.3f}"` is a Gini of
`{python} f"{gini_from_auc(auc['GBM']):.3f}"`. The insurance Gini computed
from a Lorenz curve, which we'll meet with lift charts, is a close relative.

## Comparing the models

```{python}
#| label: fig-roc-compare
#| fig-cap: "ROC curves of all three models on the test set."
ax = plot_roc(y, {m: b[m] for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
grid = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)
tpr_at = {m: np.interp(grid, *roc_points(y, b[m])[["fpr", "tpr"]].T.to_numpy()) for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}
gbm_share_above = np.mean(tpr_at["GBM"] >= tpr_at["GLM"])
```

The Null model gives everyone the same score, so its curve is the diagonal
(AUC 0.5). The GBM (AUC `{python} f"{auc['GBM']:.3f}"`) ranks better than the
GLM (AUC `{python} f"{auc['GLM']:.3f}"`). Its curve lies on or above the GLM's
at `{python} f"{gbm_share_above:.0%}"` of false positive rates. Where one curve
lies above another, that model is better *at every threshold* in that region.
When curves cross, AUC alone hides which model is better in the region you
actually operate in.

How large is an AUC of 0.71? There is no universal scale. Whether a claim
happens depends largely on chance, so even a perfect pricing model would be
far from AUC 1. Judge AUC against the Null model, a simpler baseline and what
is achievable for the problem, not against an absolute benchmark.

## What AUC does not tell you

**It ignores calibration.** AUC depends only on the *order* of the
predictions. Any transformation that keeps the order leaves it unchanged, even
one that ruins the probabilities:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-auc-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Order-preserving transformations of the GBM: same AUC, very different probabilities."
#| code-fold: false
variants = {
    "GBM": b["GBM"],
    "GBM / 10": b["GBM"] / 10,
    "GBM ^ 0.2": b["GBM"] ** 0.2,
}
pd.DataFrame({
    "AUC": {k: auc_rank(y, v) for k, v in variants.items()},
    "Average predicted probability": {k: v.mean() for k, v in variants.items()},
    "Actual claim rate": {k: y.mean() for k in variants},
}).round(3)
```

All three rank equally well, but only the first predicts claim probabilities
that resemble reality. If the probabilities themselves matter (pricing, expected
cost, the threshold formula on the previous page), measure **calibration** as
well.

**It weighs all thresholds equally.** AUC averages over the whole curve,
including regions no one would use. With 96% non-claims, a false positive rate
of just 10% already means `{python} f"{0.1 * (y == 0).sum():,.0f}"` false
alarms on the test set. If only the top few percent of scores will ever be
acted on, look at the left part of the curve, at precision–recall curves, or
at lift charts.

**It is an estimate.** The test set is a sample, so AUC has sampling
uncertainty. Before concluding that the GBM beats the GLM, we need a
confidence interval for the difference (bootstrap or DeLong's test, on a later
page).

## Takeaways

- The ROC curve shows the trade-off between catching positives (TPR) and
  false alarms (FPR) across **all thresholds**.
- AUC is the **probability of ranking a random positive above a random
  negative**: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. Gini = 2·AUC − 1.
- AUC measures **ranking only**: it says nothing about whether the
  probabilities are right.
- Under heavy imbalance, complement it with precision–recall or lift, and
  always quantify its uncertainty when comparing models.
